blocks.text: A geothermal well delivers 1 MW of heat as hot water at 90 °C, and a steelworks furnace offers 1 MW of heat at 1500 °C. By the first law the two are the same amount of energy, but the furnace heat can drive a good power plant and the 90 °C heat can drive only a poor one. Exergy is the quantity that says how much of each is actually useful. This unit defines it for heat and for a flowing stream.

blocks.markdown: Energy is conserved in every process, so the first law cannot tell us how much of the energy can be turned into work. The **second law** limits this. The maximum useful work obtainable from a system as it comes into equilibrium with its surroundings is called its **exergy** (or availability). The surroundings are taken as a large reservoir at the **dead state**: temperature $T_0$ and pressure $P_0$ (typically 25 °C and 100 kPa), at which the system can no longer produce work.

blocks.title: Exergy and the dead state
blocks.text: Exergy is the maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system or stream as it reaches the dead state ($T_0$, $P_0$, zero velocity, at ground level) while exchanging heat only with the environment at $T_0$. At the dead state the exergy is zero. Unlike energy, exergy is not conserved: it is destroyed by irreversibilities.

blocks.caption: Flow exergy per unit mass of a steady stream (kJ/kg). $h_0$ and $s_0$ evaluated at $T_0$, $P_0$; $V$ in m/s (divide $V^2/2$ by 1000 for kJ/kg); $z$ is elevation above the reference.
Ideal gas with constant $c_p$ and gas constant $R$, with temperature in K. For air $c_p = 1.005$ and $R = 0.287$ kJ/(kg K).

blocks.title: Flow exergy of compressed air
blocks.prompt: Air at 600 K and 800 kPa flows at negligible speed. The dead state is $T_0 = 300$ K and $P_0 = 100$ kPa. Taking $c_p = 1.005$ and $R = 0.287$ kJ/(kg K), find the flow exergy per kg.

steps.text: Enthalpy difference from the dead state.

blocks.answer: Flow exergy = 271.6 kJ/kg: about 90% of the enthalpy rise above the dead state (301.5 kJ/kg) could be turned into work, the rest being unrecoverable.

blocks.title: Exergy of heat transfer
blocks.text: The maximum work obtainable from heat $Q$ received at a constant source temperature $T$, using the environment at $T_0$ as the cold reservoir, is the Carnot work: $X_Q = (1 - T_0/T)\,Q$. The remainder $Q\,T_0/T$ is anergy, which cannot be converted to work.

blocks.caption: $T$ and $T_0$ in K; $Q$ in kJ gives $X_Q$ in kJ. If $T$ varies, integrate $\int (1 - T_0/T)\,\delta Q$.

blocks.title: Exergy of heat from two sources
blocks.prompt: With $T_0 = 300$ K, find the exergy of 1000 kJ of heat available at (a) 500 K and (b) 1500 K.
blocks.answer: (a) 400 kJ of work is possible; (b) 800 kJ. Heat at 1500 K has about 2.0 times the exergy of the same quantity at 500 K.

Yes: air at the dead state has large internal energy but zero exergy

blocks.caption: Comparison of energy and exergy.

blocks.markdown: **Exergy destruction.** In a real process, entropy is generated, $S_{gen} > 0$, and the exergy destroyed is $X_{dest} = T_0 S_{gen}$ (the Gouy-Stodola relation, developed in the next unit). Energy conservation tells us that all the energy is still present after a throttling process, but the exergy is reduced, because the ability to do work (to expand through a turbine) has been lost.

blocks.title: Energy is conserved; exergy is destroyed
blocks.text: A throttling valve, a heat exchanger with a finite temperature difference and a resistor heater all conserve energy exactly. They destroy exergy because they are irreversible. The first law counts quantity of energy; exergy measures its quality.

items: Heat at the ambient temperature has zero exergy.
The Carnot factor $(1 - T_0/T)$ rises toward 1 as $T$ increases.
Exergy has the same units as energy (kJ, or kJ/kg per unit mass).
The choice of dead state matters: state $T_0$ and $P_0$ explicitly.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Use kelvin in $T_0/T$ and in logarithms. Do not use the heat source's exergy factor for heat received below $T_0$ (the factor becomes negative, meaning work must be supplied, as in refrigeration). Remember $V^2/2$ is in J/kg when $V$ is in m/s.

points: Exergy is the maximum useful work relative to a dead state $(T_0, P_0)$.
Energy is conserved but exergy is destroyed by irreversibility.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes energy conservation from exergy destruction?

options.text: Exergy is conserved in every process but energy is destroyed by irreversibility
Both energy and exergy are conserved in all real processes
Energy is conserved in every process, but exergy is destroyed whenever a process is irreversible
Neither energy nor exergy is conserved in a throttling valve

questions.correctOptionText: Energy is conserved in every process, but exergy is destroyed whenever a process is irreversible

distractorRationale.d: Energy is conserved in a throttling valve.

questions.explanation: The first law makes energy conserved, so energy leaving equals energy entering. The second law makes exergy destruction positive for any real process, so the work potential falls even though the energy stays.

questions.stem: What is the exergy of heat transferred at a temperature equal to the dead-state temperature $T_0$?

options.text: Zero
Equal to the heat transferred
Negative
Infinite

distractorRationale.b: This would be true only for a source at infinite temperature.
distractorRationale.c: Negative values arise only for sources below $T_0$.
distractorRationale.d: The Carnot factor is bounded by 1.

questions.explanation: The Carnot factor is $1 - T_0/T = 0$ when $T = T_0$. Heat at ambient temperature cannot drive a heat engine with an ambient sink, so it has no exergy.

questions.stem: A stream of air at the dead-state temperature and pressure, with negligible speed and elevation, flows through a pipe. What is its flow exergy?

options.text: Equal to its enthalpy
Equal to its internal energy
Equal to $T_0 s$
Zero

distractorRationale.a: Exergy uses the difference from the dead state.
distractorRationale.c: Entropy terms are differences from the dead state.

questions.explanation: With $T = T_0$, $P = P_0$ and no kinetic or potential energy, $h = h_0$ and $s = s_0$, so $\psi = 0$. The stream is in equilibrium with the environment and cannot do work.

questions.stem: With $T_0 = 300$ K, which heat transfer has the greater exergy: 1000 kJ at 600 K or 4000 kJ at 350 K?

options.text: 1000 kJ at 600 K, with about 500 kJ of exergy compared with 571 kJ
4000 kJ at 350 K, with about 571 kJ of exergy compared with 500 kJ
They are equal, because exergy depends only on the energy
1000 kJ at 600 K, because higher temperature always means more exergy

questions.correctOptionText: 4000 kJ at 350 K, with about 571 kJ of exergy compared with 500 kJ

distractorRationale.a: The values are right but the comparison is inverted.
distractorRationale.c: Exergy depends on the source temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Quantity of heat also matters; 4000 kJ at 350 K wins here.

questions.explanation: Exergy is $(1 - T_0/T)Q$. At 600 K it is $1000\times0.5 = 500$ kJ; at 350 K it is $4000\times0.1429 = 571$ kJ, so the larger quantity of cooler heat has slightly more exergy.

questions.stem: Air at high pressure passes through an adiabatic throttling valve with negligible change in kinetic energy. What happens to its energy and its exergy?

options.text: Both energy and exergy are unchanged
Energy decreases and exergy is unchanged
Energy is conserved (enthalpy unchanged for an ideal gas) while exergy decreases
Energy decreases and exergy increases

questions.correctOptionText: Energy is conserved (enthalpy unchanged for an ideal gas) while exergy decreases

distractorRationale.a: The entropy rises, so exergy is lost.
distractorRationale.b: Energy is conserved in the valve.
distractorRationale.d: Exergy cannot increase in an adiabatic irreversible process.

questions.explanation: The steady-flow energy balance gives $h_{out} = h_{in}$, so the energy flow is unchanged. Entropy is generated, so $T_0 s$ increases at the outlet and the flow exergy falls, representing the lost ability to expand through a turbine.

questions.stem: 2500 kJ of heat is received from a source at 400 K. Taking the environment at $T_0 = 290$ K, find the exergy of this heat in kJ.
questions.explanation: The exergy of heat is $(1 - T_0/T)Q = (1 - 290/400)\times2500 = 0.275\times2500 = 687.5$ kJ. The remaining 1812.5 kJ is anergy.

questions.stem: Air leaves a compressor at 400 K and 500 kPa and flows slowly. The dead state is 300 K and 100 kPa. Use $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K) and $R = 0.287$ kJ/(kg K) (constant). Find the flow exergy in kJ/kg.

Air leaves a nozzle at 350 K and 150 kPa with a speed of 120 m/s. The dead state is 293 K and 101.3 kPa. Use $c_p = 1.005$ kJ/(kg K) and $R = 0.287$ kJ/(kg K) and neglect elevation. Calculate the flow exergy in kJ/kg, including kinetic energy.

A student states: 'A throttling valve does not lose any energy, so nothing is lost in throttling.' Explain why this statement is misleading, using the concepts of energy conservation and exergy destruction.
markingGuide: Agrees that energy is conserved: $h_{in} = h_{out}$ for adiabatic steady flow with no work
Throttling is irreversible: entropy is generated, $s_{out} > s_{in}$
Flow exergy $\psi = (h-h_0) - T_0(s-s_0)+\dots$ falls because $s$ increases at constant $h$
The lost exergy is the work that a turbine could have produced in expanding the fluid
Concludes that energy quantity is unchanged but quality (ability to do work) is degraded
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved in throttling, so no energy is lost. But entropy is generated, so exergy is destroyed by an amount $T_0 S_{gen}$, representing the work potential wasted.

questions.stem: A building is heated to 40 °C (313 K) by an electric resistance heater, with the outdoor environment at 0 °C (273 K). 1 kWh of electricity is converted entirely into heat at 40 °C. (a) Calculate the exergy of that heat. (b) What fraction of the electrical exergy is destroyed? (c) Explain what this implies about the efficiency of heating with electricity, referring to the energy and exergy views.
markingGuide: Electricity is pure work, so its exergy is 1 kWh
Energy view: the heater is 100% efficient, since all energy becomes heat
Exergy view: only about 13% of the work potential is retained, so the second-law efficiency is low
A heat pump supplies the same heat with less electrical input, so it does less exergy destruction
Concludes that matching the quality of energy supply to the demand matters
questions.explanation: The exergy of 1 kWh of heat at 313 K is 0.128 kWh, so about 87% of the electrical exergy is destroyed. The first law rates the heater at 100%, but the second law shows it wastes most of the work potential.
